title: What Is an Indoor Air Quality Assessment?
h1: What Is an Indoor Air Quality Assessment, and What Does It Check?
description: An indoor air quality assessment checks humidity, particles, ventilation and your HVAC system to find what's affecting your home's air. Here's what to expect.
quick_answer: An indoor air quality assessment is an evaluation of the air in your home and the things that affect it. A technician asks about symptoms and concerns, measures conditions like humidity, particles and carbon dioxide, inspects the HVAC system, filters and ducts, looks for moisture and odor sources, then explains the findings and options.
body:
If your home feels stuffy, smells musty, gets dusty quickly or seems to make allergies worse, the cause isn't always obvious. An assessment looks at your home as a system, including the HVAC equipment, ducts, ventilation and moisture, to figure out what's going on before you spend money on fixes.

What happens during an indoor air quality assessment?

  1. Conversation. The technician asks what you've noticed, when it happens, which rooms are affected and who in the home is bothered.
  2. Measurements. Instruments check things like temperature, humidity, airborne particles and carbon dioxide in different rooms.
  3. HVAC inspection. The filter, coil, drain pan, blower and accessible ductwork are checked for dirt, moisture and leaks.
  4. Moisture check. Signs of leaks, condensation or mold-prone areas are noted.
  5. Ventilation review. Bathroom fans, the kitchen hood and the dryer vent are checked to see if they actually remove air from the house.
  6. Findings and options. You get a plain explanation of what was found and what can be done about it.

What does the assessment measure?

  • Humidity. Too high invites mold and dust mites. Too low dries out skin and sinuses.
  • Particles. Fine particles come from dust, smoke, cooking and outdoor pollution. Readings help show whether filtration is keeping up.
  • Carbon dioxide. High readings in occupied rooms suggest the home isn't getting enough fresh air.
  • Volatile organic compounds. Some assessments measure overall VOCs from paint, furniture, cleaners and other products.
  • Temperature differences. Uneven rooms can point to duct or airflow problems.

Many technicians also check for carbon monoxide near gas appliances as a safety step.

What problems can an assessment uncover?

  • Filters that are the wrong size, the wrong type or overdue
  • Dirty coils, drain pans or blowers
  • Leaky return ducts pulling in attic, garage or crawl space air
  • Disconnected or crushed ducts in the attic
  • High humidity from an oversized AC or poor ventilation
  • Exhaust fans that vent into the attic instead of outside
  • Signs of rodent contamination near ducts or equipment
  • Smoke infiltration after wildfires or Santa Ana wind events

Who should consider an assessment?

An assessment makes sense if:

  • Someone in the home has allergies, asthma or breathing concerns
  • The house has a musty or persistent odor
  • Dust returns quickly after cleaning
  • You've had water damage, a roof leak or pests
  • You've just moved into an older home
  • Wildfire smoke got into the house
  • You've remodeled and want to know if dust spread through the ducts

How should you prepare for an assessment?

A little prep helps the technician find answers faster:

  1. Write down symptoms, odors or dust problems and when they happen.
  2. Note any past water leaks, pest problems or remodeling.
  3. Leave the filter in place so its condition can be seen.
  4. Clear access to the furnace or air handler, the attic hatch and the return grille.
  5. Avoid running air purifiers or cleaning heavily right before the visit, so readings reflect normal conditions.

Is an assessment the same as mold testing?

Not exactly. An HVAC-focused indoor air quality assessment looks at conditions and sources, such as moisture, airflow and dirty equipment. Lab mold testing collects samples and sends them to a laboratory to identify specific types and levels. If an assessment shows signs of significant mold, you may be pointed toward lab testing or a mold remediation specialist.

What happens after the assessment?

Some findings can be fixed during the visit, like a missing filter or a clogged drain. Others take a separate appointment. You should get the findings in plain terms, so you can decide what to do and when.

Depending on what's found, recommendations might include a filter upgrade, coil or duct cleaning, duct sealing, a UV light, an air purifier, a dehumidifier or humidifier, or ventilation improvements. A good technician will explain which steps make the biggest difference first and which are optional.

faqs: How long does an indoor air quality assessment take?
Most home assessments take about an hour or two, depending on the size of the home, the concerns and how much of the system needs inspecting.
Can I test my home's air quality myself?
Consumer monitors can track humidity, particles and carbon dioxide, which is useful for spotting trends. A professional assessment adds an inspection of the HVAC system and ducts to find the causes.
Will an assessment tell me if I have mold?
It can find conditions that lead to mold and visible signs of growth. Identifying specific mold types requires lab testing, which is a separate service.
What is the most common indoor air problem you find?
Dirty or poorly fitting filters, leaky return ducts and humidity problems are among the most common. Many of them are simple to fix once they're identified.
